newsitem.title: PORTUGAL: Flights back to normal as TAP strike suspended.
newsitem.headline: Flights back to normal as TAP strike suspended.

text.p: Flights returned to normal at struggling Portuguese state airline TAP-Air Portugal on Monday as pilots suspended a selective strike to give time to reach a deal with the company on working hours, officials said.
"Operations are now back to normal. Twelve flights were suspended in total over the weekend," a TAP spokeswoman, who asked not to be identified, told Reuters.
She said five flights had been cancelled on Saturday when the stoppage began and seven on Sunday as pilots refused to operate flights not scheduled at least three days in advance.
She said 1,300 passengers were stranded on Sunday, but they had all been re-routed to their destinations.
She had no figures for passengers affected on Saturday and no estimate of TAP's losses due to the strike.
After chairing talks with pilot union officials late on Sunday, Planning Minister Joao Cravinho said the pilots had called off their action for five days to let talks continue.
He added that five days should be sufficient to work out an accord on flight scheduling, which pilots say is chaotic.
"The five days were set by the union and with the experience that they have of these things, they must have thought that it was sufficient time for an agreement to be reached," he said.
The TAP spokeswoman said no talks were taking place on Monday morning, but she expected them to resume shortly.
"During this five-day truce, we expect an agreement will be reached," she said.
The stoppages were due to continue throughout August and the government had warned that they could provoke heavy losses for the company during the peak holiday season.
TAP flies international routes and to the Portuguese mid-Atlantic islands of Madeira and the Azores.
The government had said that the pilots' action was risking the survival of the airline, which hoped to return to profit in 1997 after more than two decades of losses.
It says that it is barred by agreements with the European Union from pouring any more funds into the company, which it hopes to privatise, at least partially, before the end of the century.
